rv.q: Walking With Ghosts may not necessarily be life-changing, but the spectacle of seeing this great actor reminisce about his own personal and artistic coming-of-age turns out to be surprisingly affecting indeed.
Byrne is a compelling storyteller, this collection of personal anecdotes feels essentially disjointed.

But only a fool could not see that this is a deeply honest and courageous work from an actor digging deep into what now matters to him, a self-probing of uncommon intensity that never comes off as overly egotistical or glib.
As a writer, Byrne is no Brendan Behan, but the sincerity of his voice is a fine cover for whatever artlessness it disguises.
And yet, the transition from page to stage feels undermotivated, incomplete.
Unfortunately, in this lusterless staging of “Walking with Ghosts,” there is little refuge.
“Walking With Ghosts” is a modest show, with quiet humor and gentle pathos — which is exactly why it’s so wonderful.
In its best moments, “Walking with Ghosts” has a similar effect, leaving viewers entertained and a little haunted — and perhaps just a bit more appreciative of the wonder that life and art can bring.
There is a convincing intimacy to Walking With Ghosts, but that intimacy is also slightly deceptive.

But what we are presented with, even as it is sparkled with Sinéad McKenna's supportive lighting design and Sinéad Diskin's original music and sound design, is both too much and not enough, a two-hour discourse that would best be appreciated by fans of the actor.
Fiennes is great, of course, but the play goes nowhere.
But you too often feel the actorly polish which ironically results in a distancing effect from the traumatic incidents being related.
He’s an actor who needs a big role, and the Byrne of “Ghosts” is all too ephemeral, not to mention forgettable.
Walking With Ghosts is a gift that shouldn’t be missed.
Walking with Ghosts is an intoxicating experience.

Only the actor’s gift for storytelling, with its surprising deftness at delineating the voices, brogues, and mannerisms of the multiple characters he portrays—a talent he too rarely gets to demonstrate in his stage and film roles—lift these familiar tropes to a level of compelling theatre.
But its true scale is human, which means all that’s required is Byrne and his bravery.
Luckily, Byrne proves to be an appealing, often moving raconteur, keeping our attention for the somewhat overextended 2-hour and 20-minute running time, rarely indulging in mawkish sentimentality.
I left the Theater feeling neither particularly entertained, nor motivated to learn more about who Bryne is.
